# Discussion

The analysis of nonlinear effects with latent variables requires estimation procedures that yield reliable results for inference and hypothesis testing. Most existing approaches rely on distributional assumptions that are frequently violated in applied research [@cain_etall_2017]. In this study, we compared the recently proposed LSAM with established methods across two simulation studies, evaluating their performance under different distributional, sample size, reliability conditions, and levels of model complexity. Thus, because SAM approaches for nonlinear effects have long been underrepresented in the literature [@rosseel_loh_2024] and until recently were not implemented in widely accessible software, demonstrating that a SAM procedure can provide reliable results is important for both methodological development and applied practice.

## Performance of LSAM 

The LSAM performed well across most evaluation metrics, offering a balance of accuracy and computational feasibility. Under medium and high reliability, LSAM produced unbiased estimates, adequate SEs, controlled Type I error rates, and maintained stable coverage even under non-normal conditions. It also achieved acceptable power ($\geq 80\%$) in large samples with adequate reliability in case of normal and right-skewed distributions for all nonlinear effects, while under uniform distributions quadratic terms were underpowered. Moreover, the results further underscore the practical advantages when it comes to model complexity. Convergence rates were generally high and few outlier estimates. Taken together, these findings position LSAM as a promising estimator that combines reasonable statistical performance with improved usability and software support. At the same time, limitations under low reliability highlight the need for cautious application and further methodological refinement. Although this latter point is common for all approaches. 

## Relation to Previous Findings 

Bias results for the LSAM approach were comparable to 2SMM results reported by @brandt_etall_2014, with largely unbiased estimates across conditions. LMS and QML showed a positive bias for the interaction effect and a negative bias for the quadratic effects under right-skewed distributions, consistent with @brandt_etall_2014. Under uniform settings, interaction terms remained unbiased [@lonati_etall_2024] while quadratic effects were biased. UPI also produced unbiased estimates, aligning with earlier results [@brandt_etall_2014; @marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012]. SE/SD ratio results mirrored @brandt_etall_2014, with LMS and QML showing higher efficiency. Type I error rates were generally controlled for the LSAM, whereas the LMS and QML showed an inflation in the under right-skewed condition as in @brandt_etall_2014. For UPI, Type I error rates were not inflated consistent with previous studies [@marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012], despite @brandt_etall_2014 observing inflation. LSAM and UPI also maintained a more stable performance compared to LMS and QML when it comes to coverage under non-normal conditions. For empirical power, LSAM achieved levels at or above 80% only with medium or high reliability under large samples for normal and right-skewed distributions; UPI displayed a similar pattern. LMS and QML reached power above 80% even under low reliability, as in @brandt_etall_2014, but these results must be interpreted cautiously given their inflated Type I error rates.

Moreover, these findings reinforce that estimator performance depends critically on the number and configuration of nonlinear effects. @lonati_etall_2024 found unbiased LMS estimates for a single interaction under uniform distributions, whereas including quadratic effects in the current study led to substantial bias for those effects. This extends @brandt_etall_2014, who also observed deteriorating performance as nonlinear effects increased, underscoring existing estimators’ sensitivity to model complexity and distributional violations. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine more than five nonlinear effects simultaneously, highlighting scalability challenges that arise under realistic levels of model complexity. Importantly, these challenges are not only statistical but also practical, since their impact depends on how efficiently estimation methods can be implemented and used in software.

## Recent software implements 

Indeed, the implementation of LMS and QML in C++ within *modsem* [@R-modsem] has substantially reduced computational demands, making analyses that were previously infeasible more realistic. Nevertheless, LMS remains computationally intensive, and estimation time increases rapidly with the number of nonlinear effects, so scalability continues to pose practical limitations even in optimized implementations. For UPI, the key advance lies in usability: whereas earlier applications required researchers to manually specify numerous constraints—a process that was error-prone. This shift not only reduces the risk of errors but also lowers the barrier to adoption. Yet this approach substantially increases the number of parameters. Finally, the integration of LSAM in *lavaan* [@R-lavaan] has made this new approach broadly accessible to applied researchers. Taken together, these software developments enhance the feasibility of nonlinear latent variable modeling while underscoring the need for continued caution regarding estimator assumptions, computational burden, and boundary conditions.

## Limitations and Future Research 

As with any simulation study, the present findings are conditional on the specific design factors and assumptions examined. The simulations assumed that non-normality in the indicators arose solely from the latent predictor variables. In practice, non-normality may also involve measurement errors or other structural components. Moreover, the sample sizes investigated do not include very small samples that are sometimes encountered in applied research, which may further limit generalization, especially in the case of the UPI approach. We also solely focused on distributional violations and did not address structural misspecifications. The robustness of the LSAM and some of the other approaches to these additional forms of misspecification remains an important topic for future research. Another relevant manipulation was the different population values (i.e., effect size) for nonlinear effects.

Furthermore, the literature has mainly relied on robust standard errors and minor methodological modifications to improve estimation under non-normality. For instance, reliability-corrected single-indicator LMS approaches [@cheung_lau_2017; @su_etall_2019] were proposed to reduce sensitivity to distributional violations, although @lonati_etall_2024 found notable gains primarily in small samples. Other studies have explored different ways to form product indicators [@marsh_etall_2004] and compared wald z-tests with likelihood ratio tests in terms of type I error and power [@cham_etall_2012], as these are only asymptotically equivalent [@buse_1982]. With respect to robust standard errors, we relied on standard implementations for the main analyses, but previous research largely used the robust version-despite some adjustments also modifying the test statistics as well [@savalei_rosseel_2021]. The simulation evidence suggests that they provide limited improvements [@brandt_etall_2014; @brandt_etall_2020; @marsh_etall_2004; @cham_etall_2012; @lonati_etall_2024], particularly in small samples. Hence, future research needs to explore more in-depth what this robustness is about. Last, other approaches were not explored [@bollen_1995; @boker_etall_2023; @kelava_etall_2014], some due to limited software implementations availability [@mooijaart_bentler_2010; @kelava_etall_2014].

Concerning a few estimation choices, bounded estimation procedures may enhance UPI performance in smaller samples [@de_jonckere_rosseel_2022], and future work could examine whether alpha correction procedures [@bogaert_etall_2023] or separating measurement blocks within models improves estimation for nonlinear and quadratic terms under the LSAM [@rosseel_etall_2025; @rosseel_loh_2024].
